intro.why: Viterbi is the dynamic-programming workhorse of sequence labelling: it decodes HMMs, MEMMs, CRFs and speech models alike. MEMMs show how to move from counting to feature-rich discriminative models, the step that leads to CRFs and neural taggers (M8).

symbols: Viterbi score: best path ending in state j at time t
backpointer: best previous state for (j, t)

sections.title: The decoding problem
sections.plain: Given the words, find the single most probable sequence of hidden tags.
sections.body:
An HMM supports three classic tasks: likelihood (how probable is an observation sequence? forward algorithm), decoding (which hidden sequence best explains it? Viterbi), and learning (estimate A and B; counting if tagged data exists, forward–backward otherwise). Tagging is decoding:

$$\hat t_{1:n} = \arg\max_{t_{1:n}} \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(t_i\mid t_{i-1})\,P(w_i\mid t_i)$$

Trying every sequence costs Nⁿ evaluations (45¹⁰ ≈ 3.4 × 10¹⁶ for ten words). But the score factorises into local pieces, and the best path to any state at time t only depends on the best paths to states at t − 1. That overlapping-subproblem structure is what dynamic programming exploits. (Everyday picture: planning the cheapest road trip city by city, you only ever need the cheapest way into each city.)

sections.title: The Viterbi recurrence and backpointers
sections.plain: For each tag at each word, keep only the best path that ends there and remember where it came from.
sections.body:
$$v_1(j) = \pi_j\,b_j(o_1),\qquad v_t(j) = \max_{i} v_{t-1}(i)\,a_{ij}\,b_j(o_t),\qquad bt_t(j) = \arg\max_i v_{t-1}(i)\,a_{ij}$$

Fill a lattice (trellis) column by column; at the end take $\max_j v_T(j)$ and follow backpointers to recover the path.

One cell by hand: previous column V[Verb] = 0.03, V[Noun] = 0.0015; P(Prep | Verb) = 0.2, P(Prep | Noun) = 0.3; P(in | Prep) = 1.0. From Verb 0.03 × 0.2 = 0.006; from Noun 0.0015 × 0.3 = 0.00045. Keep the max (Verb), backpointer → Verb, V[Prep] = 0.006 × 1.0 = 0.006.

Viterbi is like the forward algorithm with max in place of sum. In practice use log probabilities (sums of logs) to avoid underflow. The best whole path need not use each word's individually best tag: a locally weaker tag can win if it makes the rest of the path stronger.

sections.title: Worked Viterbi: 'the doctor is in'
sections.plain: Fill the whole table by hand and backtrace to Det Noun Verb Prep.
sections.body:
Tags Det, Noun, Verb, Prep, Adv. Transitions: P(Det | ⟨s⟩) = 0.3, Det→Noun 0.9, Det→Verb 0.01, Noun→Noun 0.2, Noun→Verb 0.4, Noun→Prep 0.3, Verb→Verb 0.05, Verb→Prep 0.2, Verb→Adv 0.1. Emissions: the|Det 0.7, doctor|Noun 0.4, doctor|Verb 0.1, is|Noun 0.1, is|Verb 0.9, in|Prep 1.0, in|Adv 0.1.

  1. "the": V[Det] = 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21 (no other tag emits "the").
  2. "doctor": Noun = 0.21 × 0.9 × 0.4 = 0.0756; Verb = 0.21 × 0.01 × 0.1 = 0.00021.
  3. "is": Verb: from Noun 0.0756 × 0.4 = 0.03024 vs from Verb 0.00021 × 0.05 ≈ 0.00001; × 0.9 = 0.027216 (bp Noun). Noun: 0.0756 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.001512 (bp Noun).
  4. "in": Prep: from Verb 0.027216 × 0.2 = 0.0054432 vs from Noun 0.001512 × 0.3 = 0.00045; × 1.0 = 0.005443 (bp Verb). Adv: 0.027216 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.000272.
  5. Best final cell Prep (0.005443); backtrace Prep ← Verb ← Noun ← Det.

Result: the/Det doctor/Noun is/Verb in/Prep. Code example ex1 reproduces every number.

sections.title: Worked Viterbi: a two-day weather HMM
sections.plain: Hidden hot/cold days from observed ice-cream counts; two columns are enough to see the max in action.
sections.body:
States H, C; π = (0.8, 0.2); A: H→H 0.6, H→C 0.4, C→H 0.5, C→C 0.5; B: P(3 | H) = 0.4, P(1 | H) = 0.2, P(3 | C) = 0.1, P(1 | C) = 0.5. Observations: 3, then 1.

  1. Day 1: v(H) = 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32; v(C) = 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02.
  2. Day 2, H: max(0.32 × 0.6, 0.02 × 0.5) = 0.192 (from H) × P(1 | H) 0.2 = 0.0384.
  3. Day 2, C: max(0.32 × 0.4, 0.02 × 0.5) = 0.128 (from H) × P(1 | C) 0.5 = 0.064.
  4. Best final: C (0.064); backpointer → H. Path H C.

Intuition: three ice creams suggest a hot day; one suggests cold, and H→C is likely enough (0.4) to switch. With more days, the lattice grows linearly while the number of paths doubles each day.

sections.title: Complexity and limits of HMMs
sections.plain: Viterbi is fast; the model itself is what limits accuracy.
sections.body:
Complexity: each of N·T cells takes a max over N predecessors, so O(N²T) time and O(NT) space for backpointers. For 45 tags and 25 words that is about 50,000 operations instead of 45²⁵ ≈ 2 × 10⁴¹ paths. Beam search keeps only the top k states per column for very large N.

HMM limits:

  • Unknown words: no emission counts; must back off to suffix, capitalisation or open-class guesses.
  • Limited context: each tag sees only the previous tag (or two in a trigram HMM), and each word depends only on its own tag.
  • No rich features: overlapping clues (suffix -ing, capitalised, contains a digit, next word) can't be added to P(word | tag) without breaking the model.
  • Sparsity: many legitimate tag/word pairs are unseen.
  • One direction: decisions can't directly use the right context; bidirectional taggers run left-to-right and right-to-left passes (or model both directions jointly).

sections.title: MEMMs: discriminative tagging with features
sections.plain: Predict each tag directly from features of the word and the previous tag, using logistic regression.
sections.body:
The HMM is generative: it models P(word | tag) and P(tag | previous tag) and inverts them with Bayes. A Maximum Entropy Markov Model is discriminative: it models the posterior directly,

$$P(t_i\mid w_i, t_{i-1}, \dots) = \frac{\exp\big(\sum_k \theta_k f_k(t_i, \text{context})\big)}{\sum_{t'}\exp\big(\sum_k \theta_k f_k(t', \text{context})\big)}$$

i.e. multinomial logistic regression applied at each position. Features are arbitrary yes/no tests: for "back", previous tag is MD; word ends in -ck; word is lowercase. For "race": previous word is "to" or "the"; word ends in -ing; word is capitalised. Weights θ are learned by gradient descent on the conditional log-likelihood of a tagged corpus.

Worked: scores VB 2.0, NN 0.5 → e² ≈ 7.39, e^0.5 ≈ 1.65, total 9.04 → P(VB) ≈ 0.82, P(NN) ≈ 0.18.

sections.title: Decoding MEMMs and the label-bias problem
sections.plain: Use Viterbi over the local probabilities, not greedy choices; beware that local normalisation can make the model ignore evidence.
sections.body:
Greedy decoding tags left to right, locking in the most probable tag at each word: fast, but an early mistake can't be undone. Viterbi over the MEMM's local probabilities $\prod_i P(t_i\mid w_i, t_{i-1})$ finds the best whole sequence (same recurrence, with $P(s\mid s', o_t)$ in place of $a_{s's}b_s(o_t)$).

Example ("the old man the boats", illustrative local probabilities): greedy picks old/JJ (0.6) then man/NN, total 0.30; Viterbi picks old/NN man/VB (0.4 × 1.0 = 0.40), the correct garden-path reading ("the old people crew the boats").

Label bias: each local distribution must sum to 1 for its previous state, so a state with few likely successors passes its probability on almost regardless of the observation. In the example, "the" after the noun "man" is ungrammatical, but P(DT | the, NN) is still 1.0, so the bad path isn't penalised. Conditional random fields (CRFs) fix this by scoring whole sequences and normalising once globally; they are still decoded with Viterbi and are used on top of neural taggers (BiLSTM-CRF, M8).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Forward vs Viterbi: replace max with sum to get P(observations), the basis of forward–backward (Baum–Welch) training.
  • Viterbi elsewhere: decoding in speech recognition, convolutional-code decoding in telecoms, gene finding, and CTC-style alignment in neural speech models.
  • Ties and zeros: add tiny smoothing or log-space −∞ handling so unseen transitions don't break the table.
  • MEMM vs CRF: same features; the CRF's global normaliser costs a forward pass per training sentence but removes label bias.

code.title: MEMM softmax, greedy vs Viterbi, label bias
code.explain: Computes the 0.82/0.18 softmax, then decodes 'the old man the boats' with hand-set local distributions: greedy gets 0.30 with old/JJ, Viterbi 0.40 with old/NN man/VB. Shows that local normalisation forces P(DT | the, NN) = 1.0 (label bias).
mistakes: Assuming greedy equals Viterbi for MEMMs.
Forgetting that each local distribution sums to 1.
code.code:
"""MEMM local softmax, greedy vs Viterbi decoding, and the label-bias effect."""
import math

# 1. Softmax over tag scores from features
scores = {"VB": 2.0, "NN": 0.5}
Z = sum(math.exp(v) for v in scores.values())
print("P(tag | features):", {k: round(math.exp(v) / Z, 2) for k, v in scores.items()})

# 2. A garden-path sentence: 'the old man the boats'
# Local MEMM distributions P(tag | word, previous tag), hand-set for illustration.
# Each row sums to 1 (local normalisation).
P = {
    ("the", "<s>"): {"DT": 1.0},
    ("old", "DT"): {"JJ": 0.6, "NN": 0.4},
    ("man", "JJ"): {"NN": 0.5, "VB": 0.5},
    ("man", "NN"): {"VB": 1.0},
    ("the", "NN"): {"DT": 1.0}, ("the", "VB"): {"DT": 1.0},
    ("boats", "DT"): {"NNS": 1.0},
}
words = "the old man the boats".split()

def local(w, prev):
    return P.get((w, prev), {})

# greedy
prev, greedy, gp = "<s>", [], 1.0
for w in words:
    dist = local(w, prev)
    if not dist: gp = 0; break
    t = max(dist, key=dist.get); greedy.append(t); gp *= dist[t]; prev = t
print("greedy :", greedy, f"score {gp:.4f}")

# Viterbi over local probabilities (product of P(t_i | w_i, t_{i-1}))
beams = {"<s>": (1.0, [])}
for w in words:
    nb = {}
    for prev, (sc, path) in beams.items():
        for t, p in local(w, prev).items():
            cand = sc * p
            if cand > nb.get(t, (0, None))[0]: nb[t] = (cand, path + [t])
    beams = nb
best = max(beams.values())
print("Viterbi:", best[1], f"score {best[0]:.4f}")

# 3. Label bias: 'the' right after the noun 'man' is ungrammatical, yet the local
# distribution P(tag | 'the', NN) must still sum to 1, so DT gets probability 1.0 and the
# greedy path is never penalised for it.
print("\nP(DT | 'the', prev=NN) =", P[("the", "NN")]["DT"], "(forced by local normalisation)")
print("A CRF scores whole sequences and normalises once, so a bad transition can lower the total.")
